description: We are a multidisciplinary team of developers, designers, and innovators passionate about space exploration, AI, and scientific discovery. We aim to transform NASA’s microgravity combustion research into meaningful, AI-powered fire safety insights for future space missions. We value collaboration, creativity, and technical excellence. We welcome participants with skills in AI/ML, data science, scientific research, UI/UX, and software engineering who are eager to contribute and learn.
summary:
PYRAXIS is an SI-powered web dashboard that turns NASA's microgravity combustion data into clear fire-safety answers for spacecraft, space stations, Moon and Mars bases, and pressurized rovers.

Moon-base air is expected to hold 30% or more oxygen at reduced pressure, where materials burn far more readily, yet NASA's evidence is spread across 24 PSI investigations and more than 60,000 files. PYRAXIS connects them into one traceable dataset of 1,709 test rows, ranks the investigations that matter for each habitat, and maps every test by oxygen and pressure. It interprets the data through the three layers of fire safety (prevention, detection and suppression) with seven machine-learning models that state their own uncertainty. It also answers plain-English questions only from cited NASA documents, and lets anyone watch a fire start, get detected and be suppressed in a live physics simulator calibrated on NASA results.

Our key finding: in NASA's public archive only 17 tests come close to Moon-base air, and none used solid cabin materials. PYRAXIS shows exactly where the evidence ends, so the next experiment, detector or extinguisher is chosen with data before astronauts depend on it.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

PYRAXIS helps aerospace researchers, engineers and students answer one question quickly: how dangerous is a fire in this habitat's air, and how would we prevent it, detect it and put it out? It is a public web dashboard built on NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) combustion data.

- Mission Control: pick a habitat (ISS, Moon base, pressurized rover, Mars habitat, spacesuit, Earth) to see how many real tests sit near its atmosphere, data-gap warnings, and the 24 combustion investigations ranked by an explainable relevance score.

- Flammability Map: every test plotted by oxygen and pressure against habitat zones; each point links back to its NASA source file and row. All data downloads as CSV.

- Investigations & Compare: objectives, hypotheses, hardware, fuels, sample sizes, test conditions, what varied between tests and what was measured, side by side.

- Fire-safety layers: Prevention (which materials keep burning), Detection (which smoke detectors see which smoke), Suppression (diluent gases, cool flames, nitrogen jets, habitat outlook), and "From data to equipment" recommendations, each naming its NASA evidence.

- Predictions: seven Gaussian-process models that give a prediction and an uncertainty range for each habitat.

- Ask the data: plain-English questions answered only from retrieved NASA passages, with numbered citations.

- Fire simulator: a live physics simulation (gravity-scaled buoyancy, oxygen- and pressure-dependent combustion, pyrolysis, smoke, photoelectric and ionisation detectors, four crew responses) comparing two habitats side by side, with an evidence meter showing how many real NASA tests back each scenario.

HOW IT WORKS

We mapped the PSI API, inventoried all 24 combustion investigations (60,826 files, 13.5 TB) and downloaded the tables, documents and instrument logs (~16 GB). One reader per investigation harmonises everything into a single SI schema of 1,709 test rows, every value traced to its source file and row. We went beyond summary tables: we hand-labelled all 122 ISS crew notes from BASS, extracted 1-second detector logs from 120 SAME/SAME-R smoke tests, and used the CFI investigators' data summary. Models are validated only on test campaigns they never saw, against simple baselines (extinction size R² 0.91; solid-material burning AUC 0.92; flame-out vs droplet burst AUC 0.83).

KEY FINDINGS

1. In NASA's public archive only 17 tests come close to Moon-base air (vs 576 near ISS air) and none used solid cabin materials; solids were only ever tested at ≤23% O2.

2. In Moon-base air, only ~9% of burning droplets are predicted to go out cleanly (vs 82% on the ISS); most burst and scatter fuel.

3. Fine smoke from wire insulation (Teflon/Kapton) was caught by the ISS photoelectric detector signal in only ~38% of tests.

4. Nitrogen jets put out only 2 of 18 flames; cutting the airflow put out 44.

5. In 124 of 146 tests an invisible cool flame kept burning after the visible flame died.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Mission planners can see where evidence ends and what to test next; equipment designers get evidence-linked recommendations (multi-sensor detectors, ventilation shut-off first, CO2 or water mist over gas jets, holding suppression until fuel cools). On Earth the same science supports water-mist extinguishers, smoke detection, firefighter gear and fire safety for home oxygen therapy. Partial gravity, absent from PSI, is bounded between microgravity and 1 g.

CREATIVITY

Uncertainty is used as a gap-finder; crew notes become data; a physics simulator calibrated on NASA findings lets anyone see the difference between fire on Earth, on the ISS and on the Moon, with an honest evidence meter beside every scenario.

TOOLS

Python (pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn, pypdf, Jupyter), Next.js/React/TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui, Apache ECharts, BM25 retrieval, Anthropic Claude API (with Groq and Hugging Face fallbacks), Vercel hosting, GitHub. Code: https://github.com/InFynnity8/Pyraxis

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Traceability (no invented values; assumptions flagged), honest validation and stated limits, inverse-flame oxygen kept separate from cabin air, and the difference between the public archive and NASA's unpublished work (e.g. Saffire-V).
